web_title: 6. The Balance Sheet, the Cash Flow & Who Owns the Company
question: Does the money on the balance sheet work for the business, and does the cash behind the profit arrive on time?

epigraph.quote: So as a result, we were only able to hit the market by February. So the funding came in late.
epigraph.author: Stallion Q1 FY27 earnings call transcript, 17 August 2026 [8]

web_blocks.html: The earlier chapters told the story in words. This one puts the numbers in tables taken from the company’s own statements and from the Screener series, then reads them together. The balance sheet tells you what the company owns and owes. The cash flow tells you whether the reported profit turned into cash. The shareholding tells you who now controls the outcome.

web_blocks.title: The profit and loss, five years and a trailing year

web_blocks.caption: Stallion: profit and loss, March 2021 to March 2026 and trailing twelve months (₹ crore, Screener) [14]
web_blocks.takeaway: Sales rose about 3.7 times between March 2021 and March 2026. The operating margin moved between 8% and 18% across the years shown, so the margin did not rise in step with sales.

web_blocks.html: Sales went from ₹118 crore to ₹431 crore in five years, and net profit went from ₹10 crore to ₹44 crore [14]. Those are real gains. The path was not smooth. Sales were nearly flat in FY24 at ₹233 crore, and profit fell to ₹15 crore that year. The trailing twelve months show sales of ₹472 crore and profit of ₹43 crore, so the strong June quarter has been partly offset by the weak September quarter.

web_blocks.title: The balance sheet changed in one year

web_blocks.caption: Stallion: balance sheet, March 2021 to September 2026 (₹ crore, Screener; Total Liabilities includes equity) [14]
web_blocks.takeaway: Equity rose from about ₹301 crore to about ₹681 crore in a single year. Borrowings stayed small throughout.

web_blocks.html: Total equity was about ₹301 crore at March 2025 and about ₹681 crore at March 2026. The audited figures agree: ₹680.60 crore, up from ₹300.84 crore [1]. Most of the increase came from the rights issue, whose net proceeds were ₹336.02 crore after issue costs [1].

web_blocks.caption: Major balance-sheet lines, March 2025 and March 2026 (₹ crore, audited) [1]
rows: The largest jump in the year, from the rights issue
Largely term deposits placed in the year [23]
Fell, so receivables did not drive the rise in cash and deposits
Small, though up more than tenfold
web_blocks.takeaway: The rise in cash and deposits is the rights issue at work. Borrowings are the one line that moved the other way, and they remain small.

web_blocks.caption: Stallion: cash flow, March 2021 to March 2026 (₹ crore, Screener) [24]
web_blocks.takeaway: Operating cash was negative in FY24 and FY25 and positive in FY26. Most of the FY26 investing outflow was deposits, not factory spending.

web_blocks.html: Operating cash flow was negative in FY24 (about ₹73 crore out) and FY25 (about ₹13 crore out) [24]. Sales were growing in those years, and that is the warning sign. Profit that does not arrive as cash is profit tied up in receivables and inventory. In FY26 operating cash flow turned positive at ₹39.36 crore [1]. One good year is not yet a habit.

Investing cash flow for FY26 shows as about −₹253 crore on Screener. The audited statements split it. About ₹205 crore went to net fixed-deposit placements, and about ₹49 crore went to property, plant and equipment, intangibles and work in progress [23]. This is the same correction made in chapter 3. Most of the outflow was parking cash, not building plants.

web_blocks.caption: FY26 cash sources and uses, largest items (₹ crore, audited) [1][23]
rows: Net proceeds of the rights issue
Property, plant and equipment, intangibles and work in progress
web_blocks.takeaway: These are the largest lines, not a full reconciliation. Taxes, interest and other items sit elsewhere in the audited cash-flow statement [23].

web_blocks.title: Returns on capital, and why the ratio fell

web_blocks.caption: Stallion: return and working-capital ratios, March 2021 to March 2026 (Screener) [24]
web_blocks.takeaway: Return on capital employed fell from 55% in March 2022 to 12% in March 2026. Part of that is arithmetic, because a larger equity base spreads the same profit more thinly.

web_blocks.html: Return on capital employed was 55% in March 2022 and 12% in March 2026 [24]. The March 2022 figure came from a much smaller equity base, so the fall is partly arithmetic. A large part of the new equity sits in deposits earning interest rather than in plant. Screener’s return on equity for the latest year is 8.93%, and its three-year figure is 11.4% [14]. Neither is a verdict on the business. Both say that the new capital has not yet been put to work at the level the old business earned.

web_blocks.caption: Shareholding pattern, March 2025 to September 2026, with shareholder count (Screener) [15]
web_blocks.takeaway: The promoter stake fell by about 20 percentage points between September 2025 and March 2026. The sources record the change, but I did not verify its cause in the filings I read, so treat it as a question to put to management.

web_blocks.region_era: United States, FY2018 to FY2019, generic drugs after a distribution partner’s agreement expired
web_blocks.mechanism: One product sold through a partner was about 37% of sales. The partner agreement expired and was not renewed, receivables ran above the company’s own expected range, and gross margin fell in the same year as a large impairment and loss.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: The partner’s product sales were $253.1 million (37% of net sales) in fiscal 2018 and $202.5 million (31%) in fiscal 2019 [29]. Gross margin fell from 42% to 37%, the operating loss was $262.3 million including $375.4 million of impairment, and net income of $28.7 million became a net loss of $272.1 million [28].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: A single-product business with a long cash cycle can move from profit to a large loss in one year. Stallion’s R-32 is its main product, and its cash conversion cycle is about 180 days, so this shape is the downside to test, not a remote case.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
paragraphs: Read the balance sheet as a question, not an answer. The rights issue made the company safer against debt, and it did that well. It does not, by itself, make the earnings safer. The question for the next two years is whether the new money turns into plants that earn, and whether it does so before the cash is needed elsewhere.

Then read the shareholding table as a list of questions. A falling promoter stake could be a choice, a funding need, or something else. Ask management which it is, and write the answer down next to the date.

book_paragraphs: Now the balance sheet and the cash flow. These are the statements that tell you whether a company’s profit is real, and how much room it has to absorb a bad year. I will keep to the tables that the company’s own filings and the Screener series support, and I will say where each number came from.

Start with the profit and loss. Sales rose from about 118 crore in March 2021 to about 431 crore in March 2026. Net profit rose from about 10 crore to about 44 crore. Those are real gains. But the path was not smooth. In FY24 sales were almost flat and profit fell to 15 crore. An operating margin that moves between 8 and 18 percent from one year to the next is not a stable business, however good the best year looks.

The rights issue changed the balance sheet more than anything else in the record. Equity went from about 301 crore a year earlier to about 681 crore. The net proceeds were about 336 crore. Most of that money did not go straight into factories. It went into bank balances and fixed deposits. That is a sensible place for cash that is waiting, but it is not a return. Until the money goes into plants that earn, it earns only interest, and the return on the whole capital base falls. That is part of why return on capital employed dropped from 55 percent in March 2022 to 12 percent in March 2026. The 2022 figure came from a much smaller equity base, so you should not read the whole fall as a collapse.

Cash flow tells the same story from another angle. Operating cash was negative in FY24 and FY25. In those years the company reported profit, but the profit was sitting in receivables and inventory rather than in the bank. FY26 was the first year in the record with a clearly positive operating cash flow, at about 39 crore. You should wait for a second positive year before you call that a habit.

The investing outflow looks alarming in the summary numbers, at about 253 crore. Read the audited statements, and most of it was fixed-deposit placement, about 205 crore. Spending on plants and equipment was about 49 crore. The difference matters. A company that parks cash in deposits is keeping its options open. A company that spends it on plants is building capacity. Stallion did the first in FY26, and the second is still ahead of it.

The sources and uses table is a useful habit. Put the big inflows on one side: the rights issue, the operating cash, the new borrowing. Put the big outflows on the other: the deposits and the plant spending. The two sides do not tie to the penny, because taxes, interest and other lines sit elsewhere in the audited statements. The largest lines are enough to show where the money went, and in FY26 most of it went into deposits.

Look at the working-capital ratios as a set. Debtor days fell to 66 in March 2026, from 102 a year earlier, which is the improvement that matters most. Inventory days stayed high at 134. Payable days are very low at 19, which means the company pays its suppliers quickly, and that is one reason the cash conversion cycle is still about 180 days. A business that buys most of its inputs from abroad, as chapter 3 showed, needs that cycle to stay under control, and a supply problem would show up there first.

Then the ownership. Promoters held 67.90 percent until September 2025. By March 2026 they held 47.80 percent, and the public held just over half. The number of shareholders rose from about 43,000 to about 66,700. A wider base can be good for trading and for governance. But a promoter stake that falls by twenty points in six months is a change you should understand before you rely on the company’s own account of its plans. I have not verified the cause in the filings I read. A rights issue may explain part of it. I did not confirm that it explains all of it.

For the failure case, look at Lannett, a United States generics company, in its fiscal 2018 and 2019. About 37% of its net sales in fiscal 2018 came from one product, levothyroxine, sold through a distribution partner. The partner agreement expired on 23 March 2019 and was not renewed, and that product fell to 31% of sales. Gross margin fell from 42% to 37%, and the company reported a net loss of $272.1 million against a profit of $28.7 million a year earlier. Its own filing also showed receivables above the expected range in June 2018, which the company partly put down to the timing of orders. The lesson matches the Stallion one: a single product and a stretched cash cycle can turn a profitable year into a large loss quickly.

The September 2026 quarter is not a balance-sheet number, but it matters to the balance sheet. Other income of 3.34 crore was larger than operating profit of 2.99 crore. When the operating business earns less than the interest on the cash, the reported quarter is being carried by the balance sheet. That is a reason to watch the next quarter’s operating profit, not the total profit line.

Before you move on, write down three numbers: the operating cash flow for the coming year, the fixed-deposit balance and what it is earmarked for, and the promoter stake at the next filing. Those three will tell you more about the balance sheet than any single ratio.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Keep a single page with three lines: operating cash, deposits and what they are for, and the promoter stake. Read it each quarter. A balance sheet changes slowly, and you only notice the change if you wrote the last number down.
